newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions confident of labor deal victory.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions confident of labor deal victory.

text.p: Argentina's top labor boss left a meeting with President Carlos Menem Monday confident that unions would win their way on workplace reforms agreed with the government despite employer protests.

Representatives of the powerful Group of Eight business chambers were due to have their turn with the Peronist Menem Monday evening, but CGT (labor federation) chief Rodolfo Daer said that unions would make no concessions.

Daer told reporters he was "more sure than ever the spirit of the agreement we signed with the government is firm. We are not going to accept changes...there is no possibility of a modification because a change to a comma or an accent would change the content of the agreement."

But he said that Menem assured him he would try to sway the business chiefs and have them give their blessing to the package of reforms to make working contracts more flexibile and cut Argentina's relatively high employment costs.
"I am convinced that the (government) has the political will to exhaust all means to reach consensus," Daer said.
The Group of Eight want to air their grievances to Menem about the "Act of Agreement" that the government signed with the CGT late last month and plans to send to Congress.

Business complains that the Act is the ineffectual ghost of the government's original plans for far-reaching labor reforms, which Menem tried to pass by decree but which were rejected as unconstitutional by the courts.
The government then set up three-way negotiations with business and labor, but the talks led nowhere.
The agreement with the CGT goes back on Menem's original plans to scrap centralized wage talks and to swap redundancy payments for unemployment insurance plans.
With mid-term congressional elections looming in October, the government is under pressure to come up with something to bring down the 17.3 percent unemployment rate.
A group of Peronist congressmen said on the weekend they would propose a bill to raise $1.2 billion with a bond issue backed by tax debts to subsidize 600,000 new jobs.

A chink of light for the government appeared Monday, with comments by an Economy Ministry source that Greater Buenos Aires unemployment has fallen to 17.3 percent, down from 18.8 percent at the time of the last official figures in October.
